title: Unit Vectors along the Radius and the Tangent
theory:
**Big idea:** Instead of fixed X and Y directions, use two directions that move with the particle: **outward along the radius** and **along the tangent**.

**The two unit vectors at point P (angular position θ)**
- **Radial unit vector** (outward): **e_r = i cos θ + j sin θ**
- **Tangential unit vector** (direction of increasing θ): **e_t = –i sin θ + j cos θ**

They are perpendicular to each other, and both turn as the particle moves round.

**Position and velocity**
- Position: **r** = r **e_r** = r(i cos θ + j sin θ)
- Differentiating: **v** = rω(–i sin θ + j cos θ) = **rω e_t**

So the velocity is **always along the tangent**, and its magnitude is v = rω.

**Quick checks**
| θ | e_r | e_t |
|---|---|---|
| 0° | **i** | **j** |
| 90° | **j** | –**i** |
| 180° | –**i** | –**j** |

> 💡 Since the velocity is always tangent to the circle, a stone whirled on a string flies off **along the tangent** when the string breaks, not straight outward.

questions.prompt: The velocity of a particle moving in a circle is always directed:

options.text: Along the tangent to the circle

questions.explanation: **v** = rω **e_t**, which is always along the tangent.

questions.prompt: The radial unit vector at angular position θ is:

options.text: i cos θ + j sin θ
i sin θ + j cos θ

questions.explanation: e_r points from the centre towards the particle: (cos θ, sin θ).

questions.prompt: At θ = 0°, the tangential unit vector e_t (direction of increasing θ) equals:
The angle between e_r and e_t at any point on the circle is:
questions.explanation: (cos θ)(–sin θ) + (sin θ)(cos θ) = 0, so they are perpendicular.

questions.prompt: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string, and the string suddenly breaks. The stone flies off:

options.text: Along the tangent at the point where it was released

questions.explanation: With no force left, it keeps moving with its last velocity, which was along the tangent.
